newsitem.title: CHINA: As China prepares to cremate Deng, worries emerge.
newsitem.headline: As China prepares to cremate Deng, worries emerge.

text.p: China's leaders made final preparations on Sunday for funeral rites for deceased patriarch Deng Xiaoping, moving forward with a smooth show of unity despite hints of tightening political tensions beneath the surface.

Deng, who died last Wednesday aged 92, will be cremated on Monday after family members and the top leadership pay their final respects to his body in a small private ceremony at a Beijing military hospital.

Authorities imposed tight security around the capital and especially in Tiananmen Square, the vast central space where the country will commemorate Deng with official memorial rites at the Great Hall of the People on Tuesday.

Chinese sources said the military had been placed on alert to deal swiftly with potential ethnic unrest or any other threat to internal stability as China negotiates the delicate first days of political transition.

So far, the public has seen a graceful display of unanimity at the top of China's communist power structure, with the supreme leader's hand-picked successor Jiang Zemin vowing to keep China on the road of economic reform and development plotted by his mentor.

But Chinese political analysts said cracks were appearing in the facade and Jiang, who holds the top state, party and military posts and is now unarguably the most powerful man in China, may be trying to throw his weight around too soon.
"Jiang Zemin is not a strongman. He's no Mao Zedong and he's no Deng Xiaoping," said one Chinese analyst. "He can't do whatever he likes."

In one sign that old rivalries are beginning to resurface, a Chinese source said on Sunday that Jiang had refused a request from his predecessor, disgraced former Communist Party chief Zhao Ziyang, to join the 10,000 mourners at Deng's funeral.

The Soviet-trained technocrat, who replaced Zhao as party chief after he sided with the students in the ill-fated 1989 pro-democracy protests, rejected Zhao's request even though Deng's family had agreed to let him attend, the source said.

Surveillance of Zhao, who remains under virtual house arrest but is sometimes allowed to travel outside Bejing, was expected to tighten in the run-up to a crucial party congress later this year, the source said, as Jiang tries to cement his hold on power after the death of his powerful protector.

On the other side of the political divide, China's top conservative ideologue, Deng Liqun, was excluded from the high-profile funeral committee for Deng at the request of the dead man's family, Chinese sources said.
Deng Liqun earned the family's scorn when he openly criticised the patriarch for making a 1992 tour of southern China that kick-started a faltering economy, the source said.
Deng Liqun, who is not related to the late paramount leader, was China's propaganda chief for several years under Deng and had been personally loyal to him for years.

Even as Deng lay on his deathbed, signs emerged of opposition to Jiang, who surprised many analysts by waiting a scant two days before declaring that he could outperform his mentor in running China's affairs.

China's most conservative magazine, Zhongliu, or Mainstay, issued a stinging attack on a book seen as pro-Jiang in its February edition. It was quickly banned, according to sources in the publishing industry.
"It was the first cannon fired by leftists at Jiang Zemin," a political analyst said of the magazine, mouthpiece of Communist Party hardliners.
Despite signs of political jockeying at the top, for most of China's 1.2 billion people the fourth day of official mourning for Deng passed uneventfully.

In Shanghai and other cities, shoppers crowded state bookstores to buy posters and biographies of the dead leader, while in a church in Beijing Chinese Catholics offered prayers for the soul of a man who long professed atheism.
"I hope God will take care of him," one worshipper said.
In Deng's home village of Paifang in Sichuan province, officials reported that the flood of pilgrims to the departed leader's birthplace continued unabated.
One official reached by telephone said more than 200,000 people had come, some from as far as Hong Kong, 1,150 km (715 miles) away, or even Taiwan, about 1,650 km (1,000 miles) distant.
"There is an endless flow of people in here, the lines are reaching into the streets," he said.
